title: GoTranscript Transcription Test

exam.scoring: Practice bank: six sessions of 19 items, pass mark 70% per session. GoTranscript's own test works differently: a guidelines quiz that must be passed with 100% correct (each question can have one or more correct answers), then a test job transcribed in clean verbatim with no timestamping.

content_provenance: Original practice items authored directly from GoTranscript's public transcriber guidelines - the instructions GoTranscript tells applicants to read before taking its transcription test (https://gotranscript.com/transcription-guidelines). Not a capture of past test questions, and GoTranscript does not endorse this bank.

guide.name: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines
guide.structure: Part 1: guidelines quiz, 100% correct required, one or more correct answers per question. Part 2: test job transcribed in clean verbatim, no timestamping.

items.stem: Which statement matches GoTranscript's definition of full verbatim?
options: The text is transcribed exactly as it sounds and includes all the utterances of the speakers
The text keeps the speaker's meaning but drops fillers and stutters
The text is edited for grammar and readability
Only the interviewer's words are transcribed
items.explanation: The guidelines define full verbatim as text transcribed exactly as it sounds, including all utterances of the speakers. Nothing is cleaned up.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Text format descriptions: Full verbatim

items.stem: In full verbatim, which set of things does the transcriber transcribe as spoken?
options: Speech errors, false starts, filler words, slang words, stutters and repetitions
items.explanation: Full verbatim includes speech errors, false starts, filler words, slang words, stutters and repetitions, because the text is transcribed exactly as it sounds.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Full verbatim: speech errors, false starts, filler words, slang, stutters, repetitions

items.stem: Which of these does a clean verbatim transcript leave out?
options: Speech errors, stutters and filler words
items.explanation: Clean verbatim removes speech errors, false starts (unless they add information), stutters, repetitions and filler words, but expressions, contractions and emphasis repetitions stay.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Clean verbatim

items.stem: A speaker says 'Oh my God'. What must the transcriber do in either verbatim format?
options: Delete it, because it is an exclamation
Replace it with a neutral phrase
items.explanation: Expressions such as 'Oh my God', 'Oh dear', 'Oh my', 'Oh boy' and 'Oh' should be kept regardless of the verbatim type.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Expressions should be kept regardless of verbatim type

items.stem: In a clean verbatim transcript, a speaker says 'gonna'. How must it be written?
items.explanation: Slang words must be expanded in clean verbatim: 'going to' instead of 'gonna'. The other spellings are not words at all.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Slang words must be written as 'going to' instead of 'gonna'

items.stem: Which set of slang expansions is exactly right for a clean verbatim transcript?
options: gotcha becomes gotten you; 'cause becomes cos
gotcha becomes got you; 'cause becomes because; wanna becomes want to
gotcha stays gotcha; 'cause becomes because; wanna becomes want to
gotcha becomes got you; 'cause becomes cause; wanna becomes wan na
items.explanation: The guidelines require 'got you' instead of 'gotcha', 'because' instead of ''cause' and 'want to' instead of 'wanna'.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Slang words must be written as 'got you' instead of 'gotcha', 'because' instead of ''cause'

items.stem: In clean verbatim, the reactions 'yeah', 'yep', 'yap', 'yup' and 'mm-hmm' are all written as which word?
items.explanation: The guidelines say these reactions 'must be written as "yes"'. The clean verbatim example renders Maya's 'Yeah.' and 'Yep.' as 'Yes.'
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - 'Yeah', 'yep', 'yap', 'yup', 'mm-hmm' must be written as 'yes'

items.stem: In clean verbatim, when may a 'yeah' or 'yes' reaction be kept in the text?
options: Only at the start of a paragraph
When it answers a given question
items.explanation: The clean verbatim note says to omit all the 'yeah' and 'yes' reactions to retain a fluent text, unless they are answers to given questions.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Note: For CV, omit all the 'yeah', 'yes' reactions unless they are answers to given questions

items.stem: How must the word 'alright' be written in a clean verbatim transcript?
items.explanation: The guidelines state that 'alright' must be written as 'all right'.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - 'alright' must be written as 'all right'

items.stem: How must the affirmative 'OK' or 'Ok' be spelled?
items.explanation: Never spell 'Ok' or 'OK'. It must always be spelled as 'Okay'.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Never spell 'Ok' or 'OK'. It must always be spelled as 'Okay'

items.stem: In clean verbatim, a speaker repeats a word for emphasis: 'No, no, no.' How is it handled?
items.explanation: Clean verbatim removes repetitions in general, but keeps repetitions of words that express emphasis, such as 'No, no, no.' or 'I am very, very happy.'
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Repetitions: keep repetitions of words that express emphasis

items.stem: A speaker says 'If you know what I mean, we should leave.' What should the transcriber do in clean verbatim?
options: Use [inaudible 00:00:00] when speech cannot be heard due to poor recording or noise
Use [unintelligible 00:00:00] when speech can be heard but cannot be understood due to manner of speech or accent
Use [unintelligible] when there is too much background noise
items.explanation: The guidelines say not to remove filler words if they change the meaning of the phrase, and to be mindful of context because some filler words are not fillers at all.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Do not remove filler words if they change the meaning of the phrase

items.stem: In clean verbatim, when is a false start kept rather than removed?
options: When it is longer than five words
items.explanation: Clean verbatim removes false starts unless they add information. The guidelines' example is 'Sage is-- You're right, that boy is my son.'
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Clean verbatim: False starts (unless they add information)

items.stem: In full verbatim, which forms does the guidelines say to use for the affirmative and the negative?
options: Mm-hmm and Mm (affirmative) or Mm-mm (negative); Uh-huh (affirmative) or Uh-uh (negative)
Mm-hmm (affirmative) or Mm (negative); Uh-huh (affirmative) or Uh-uh (negative)
items.explanation: Only these forms are used for the affirmative/negative: Mm-hmm, Mm (affirmative) or Mm-mm (negative), and Uh-huh (affirmative) or Uh-uh (negative).
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Only use these forms for the affirmative/negative

items.stem: A speaker says 'ain't gonna change it'. How must it be written?
options: Expanded to 'is not going to change it'
Kept as 'ain't going to change it'
items.explanation: Never change spoken contractions, in either verbatim format. The guidelines list y'all, ain't, don't, can't and it's.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Never change spoken contractions

items.stem: In full verbatim, a speaker stutters: 'I-I went to the bank last Tu-Thursday.' How is it transcribed?
options: As 'I went to the bank last Thursday'
As 'I went to the bank' with a [pause 00:00:00] mark
Omitted, because stutters carry no information
items.explanation: Full verbatim keeps stutters exactly as spoken; the guidelines' example is 'I-I went to the bank last Tu-Thursday.'
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Full verbatim: Stutters

items.stem: In a full verbatim file, how are slang words such as 'kinda', 'betcha' and 'dunno' handled?
options: Expanded to 'kind of', 'bet you' and 'do not know'
items.explanation: Full verbatim includes slang words exactly as they are said. The expansion rules ('going to', 'got you', 'want to', 'because') belong to clean verbatim.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Full verbatim: Slang words

items.stem: In clean verbatim, a sentence starts with the conjunction 'But': 'But I forgot my umbrella.' What does the guidelines say to do?
options: Keep the sentence exactly as spoken
Expand the sentence instead: 'I forgot my umbrella'
Mark it as a false start
Start a new paragraph before the sentence
items.explanation: Clean verbatim should avoid starting phrases with conjunctions. If the conjunction is really needed, expand the sentence, e.g. 'I went outside but forgot to bring my umbrella.'
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Avoid starting phrases with conjunctions in clean verbatim

items.stem: Which group of words does the guidelines list as filler words for clean verbatim?
options: uh, um, you know, like, I mean, so, kind of, well, sort of
please, thank you, sorry, excuse me
items.explanation: The clean verbatim filler list is uh, um, you know, like, I mean, so, kind of, well, sort of. Be mindful of context: some of these do not always function as filler words.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Clean verbatim: filler words

items.stem: What is the required format for a timestamp in a GoTranscript file?
items.explanation: Timestamping time format must be [00:00:00]. Parentheses are never used; square brackets are used for notes and marks.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Timestamping time format must be: [00:00:00]

items.stem: How must a timestamp be formatted in terms of weight?
options: Everything with a timestamp (pause, inaudible, unintelligible, time marks) should be bolded
Only speaker labels and timestamp marks should be bolded; nothing else
Only section headers should be bolded
items.explanation: The timestamping format is always in bold, and everything that carries a time-stamp must be bolded.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Timestamping time format must be: [00:00:00] (always in bold)

items.stem: When a client requests interval timestamping, how often must timestamps be inserted?
options: Only at the start of the file
items.explanation: The guidelines list 'Every 2 minutes' as one of the two timestamping types.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Timestamping types: Every 2 minutes

items.stem: GoTranscript offers interval timestamping and one other timestamping type. What is the second type?
options: Only for the first speaker in the file
items.explanation: The two timestamping types are 'every 2 minutes' and 'every time the speaker changes'.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Timestamping types: Every time the speaker changes

items.stem: A transcriber is assigned the 20 to 30 minute part of a file. Where should the timestamps begin?
options: If the speaker’s name is mentioned at some point, use it as the speaker’s label
If the full name is used, the last name can later be dropped (optional)
Speaker labels can never be shortened
Only numeric labels like Speaker 1 may be used
items.explanation: Always consider the whole file when timestamping: for the 20-30 minutes part, timestamping starts at 20, not 00.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Always consider the whole file when you are time stamping

items.stem: A comment on the file says 'Please use the embedded time'. What must the transcriber do?
options: Ignore the comment and use the tool timer
Download the file and watch the video to read the burned-in time
Ask the client to re-upload the file
items.explanation: When a comment asks for the embedded or burned-in time, the transcriber must download the file and watch the video to use the correct time.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Note about embedded or burned-in time

items.stem: A speaker's name appears in the title of the file. How should that name be used?
options: Follow customer requests for spoken directions such as a new paragraph, comma, or period when possible
Always transcribe every instruction spoken by the customer
items.explanation: If the speaker's name is mentioned at some point or indicated in the title of the file, use it as the speaker's label.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Speaker labels: use the name mentioned in the file or indicated in the title

items.stem: What do the guidelines say about speaker labels when only one person is speaking?
items.explanation: Always use a speaker label even if there is only one speaker.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Always use a speaker label even if there is only one speaker

items.stem: Which label is the most descriptive choice for the person who hosts a talk show?
items.explanation: Make each speaker's role as descriptive as possible: Interviewer, Interviewee, Participant 1, Host, Facilitator, Caller, Receiver and so on.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Make each speaker's role in the audio as descriptive as possible

items.stem: A speaker is introduced as 'Dr. David Butterfield'. What may the transcriber do later in the file?
options: Add a second label style for the same person
Drop the last name and the title, for example to 'David'
items.explanation: Later in the transcription the last name can be dropped, and the same goes for titles such as Doctor or Pastor. This is optional and is not considered an error.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Speaker labels: dropping the last name and titles is optional

items.stem: The transcriber cannot tell which of two similar voices is speaking. What should be added before the speaker label?
items.explanation: If you cannot identify exactly who is speaking, add a question mark before the speaker label, for example ?David, ?Interviewee 2, ?Speaker 3.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - add a question mark before the speaker label

items.stem: How must a speaker label be written in the transcript?
options: Name in quotes, then a hyphen
Name in capitals, then a tab
Name in bold, followed by a colon and a space
items.explanation: Speaker labels must be written in bold, followed by a colon and a space.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Speaker labels must be written in bold, followed by a colon and space

items.stem: Which key must never be used after a speaker label?
items.explanation: NEVER use the Tab button, only one click of the Space button, after the speaker label.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - NEVER use the Tab button, only one click of the Space button

items.stem: What is the maximum recommended length of a paragraph in a transcript?
options: Commas and periods always go inside the quotation marks
Quotations are introduced by a comma, not a colon
Periods always go outside the quotation marks
Quotations must never use double quotation marks
items.explanation: Longer speeches should be separated into smaller paragraphs, and paragraphs shouldn't be longer than 500 symbols (about 100 words or 3-4 lines in the transcription tool).
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Paragraphs shouldn't be longer than 500 symbols

items.stem: A file contains a long section of sung lyrics. How should it be transcribed?
options: Like a poem, broken into lines
items.explanation: The 500-symbol paragraph limit has one exception: transcribe lyrics like a poem.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Exception: transcribe lyrics like a poem

items.stem: A speaker joins long stretches of thought with 'and', 'so' and 'but'. What should the transcriber do?
options: Create sentence divisions at the conjunctions and cut them out when they are not needed
Keep everything in one very long paragraph
items.explanation: It is often a good idea to create sentence divisions where a speaker uses conjunctions, and to cut out the conjunctions when they are not necessary. Divide sentences in the way that makes the meaning clearest to the reader.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: conjunctions and sentence divisions

items.stem: Which pair of rules applies to every sentence in a transcript?
options: It ends with a punctuation mark and it starts with a capital letter
It ends with a comma and it starts with a capital letter
It ends with a period and it starts in lower case
It ends with a question mark and it starts with a capital letter
items.explanation: Every sentence should end with a punctuation mark, and the beginning of every sentence should be capitalized. The only exceptions to the closing punctuation are a double dash (an incomplete sentence) and an inaudible or unintelligible mark.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: sentence punctuation and capitalisation

items.stem: Which two marks does the guidelines forbid in a GoTranscript transcript?
options: Round brackets instead of square brackets, and exclamation marks
Square brackets instead of round brackets, and semicolons
Round brackets instead of square brackets, and colons
items.explanation: Never use () instead of [], and never use exclamation marks.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Never use () instead of []; never use exclamation marks

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated the way the guidelines require?
options: Jack tried a new diet, but still gained weight.
Jack tried a new diet but he still gained weight.
Jack tried a new diet, but he still gained weight.
Jack tried a new diet but, he still gained weight.
items.explanation: If the conjunction and, for, or, nor, so or yet precedes an independent clause, use a comma before the conjunction: 'Jack tried a new diet but he still gained weight.'
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: comma before a coordinating conjunction

items.stem: When is [inaudible 00:00:00] the correct mark?
options: When the speaker's accent makes the words hard to understand
When a word is missing from the audio
When speech cannot be heard because of poor recording or noise
When the audio contains a foreign language
items.explanation: Use [inaudible 00:00:00] when speech cannot be heard due to poor recording or noise. The keyboard shortcut is Ctrl + K.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: [inaudible 00:00:00] (Ctrl + K)

items.stem: When is [unintelligible 00:00:00] the correct mark?
options: When the recording is too quiet to hear anything
When the audio was cut during editing
When two people speak at the same time
When speech can be heard but cannot be understood, for example because of the speaker's accent
items.explanation: Use [unintelligible 00:00:00] when speech can be heard but cannot be understood because of the speaker's manner of speech or accent. The keyboard shortcut is Ctrl + I.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: [unintelligible 00:00:00] (Ctrl + I)

items.stem: Which pairing of mark and keyboard shortcut is correct in the GoTranscript tool?
options: [inaudible 00:00:00] is Ctrl + K and [unintelligible 00:00:00] is Ctrl + I
[inaudible 00:00:00] is Ctrl + I and [unintelligible 00:00:00] is Ctrl + K
[inaudible 00:00:00] is Ctrl + M and [unintelligible 00:00:00] is Ctrl + D
[inaudible 00:00:00] is Ctrl + U and [unintelligible 00:00:00] is Ctrl + N
items.explanation: The guidelines give Ctrl + K for [inaudible 00:00:00] and Ctrl + I for [unintelligible 00:00:00].
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: keyboard shortcuts for the inaudible and unintelligible tags

items.stem: A word cannot be made out. Which markings are you allowed to use?
options: Any descriptive note you like, such as [garbled 00:00:00]
items.explanation: Mark the audio as inaudible or unintelligible and specify the time. Do NOT make up your own markings: only [inaudible 00:00:00] and [unintelligible 00:00:00] are allowed.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: do not make up your own markings

items.stem: What must an inaudible or unintelligible mark always include?
options: The time at which it occurs
items.explanation: If you cannot hear what word is being said, mark that as inaudible or unintelligible and specify the time, for example [inaudible 00:04:24].
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: specify the time

items.stem: In which format must significant sound events be noted?
options: Only when the client asks for them
In either format, regardless of the verbatim type
items.explanation: Sound events that are significant to the audio should also be noted regardless of format.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: noted regardless of format

items.stem: How is a sound event such as a laugh written in the transcript?
options: In round brackets, with a timestamp
In square brackets, without a timestamp
In square brackets, with a timestamp
As a plain sentence in the speaker's line
items.explanation: Use brackets [ ] for notes such as [laughs] and do not put timestamps in sound events.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: use brackets, do not put timestamps

items.stem: Which description of a correctly written sound-event note is accurate?
options: It may be any length as long as it is accurate
Present or progressive tense, at most two words, grammatically correct and in lower case
Past tense, at most four words, in capitals
Present tense, at most two words, capitalised at the start of a sentence
items.explanation: Sound-event notes must be in present and/or progressive tense, concise, must not exceed two words, must be grammatically correct, and must be written in lower case regardless of the position in a sentence.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: tense, length and capitalisation

items.stem: Which sound-event note follows the guidelines exactly?
items.explanation: The note must be in lower case, at most two words and grammatically correct: [laughs].
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: lower case, concise, no more than two words

items.stem: A speaker laughs during their own sentence. Where does the note go?
options: On its own line, below the speech
On the same line as the speaker's words
At the end of the file
items.explanation: Sounds that the speaker makes - a finger snap, a laugh, a chuckle - are written on the same line as that speaker's words.
items.reference: GoTranscript step-by-step guide to taking the GoTranscript transcription test - sound events made by the speaker

items.stem: The recording contains chorus laughter, applause, cheering, a ringing phone and coughing. Where do those sounds belong?
options: On the same line as the speaker's words
items.explanation: Sounds that are not made by the speaker - chorus laughter, applause, cheering, a ringing phone, coughing - are always written on a separate line.
items.reference: GoTranscript step-by-step guide to taking the GoTranscript transcription test - sound events not made by the speaker

items.stem: When is [background noise] written on the same line as the speech rather than on its own line?
options: Never; it is always on its own line
When a significant unidentified sound occurs while the speaker is talking
When the file is a full verbatim file
When the client asks for timestamps
items.explanation: Use [background noise] on a separate line for ambiance noise, and on the same line if a significant unidentified sound occurs while the speaker is talking.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: [background noise]

items.stem: Where may the marks [crosstalk] and [silence] be placed?
options: Only on the same line as the speech
On a separate line or on the same line, wherever they occur
items.explanation: [crosstalk] and [silence] can be placed on a separate line or on the same line wherever they occur.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: [crosstalk], [silence]

items.stem: How long must a pause be for [silence] to be used?
options: Not less than 4 seconds and not longer than 10 seconds
Not less than 1 second and not longer than 30 seconds
Not less than 10 seconds and not longer than 60 seconds
Any length, as long as it is noted
items.explanation: [silence] is used to demonstrate a short pause in speech: not less than 4 seconds but not longer than 10 seconds.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: [silence] duration

items.stem: What is required for a pause to be marked as [pause 00:00:00]?
options: It must be longer than 10 seconds, bolded, time-stamped and always on a separate line
It must be longer than 4 seconds and may sit inside the speaker's line
It must be time-stamped but never bolded
It may be marked only when the client requests timestamps
items.explanation: [pause 00:00:00] is bolded and time-stamped, is used for a pause that is longer than 10 seconds, and is always on a separate line.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: [pause 00:00:00]

items.stem: The audio has been cut or edited. Which mark is used?
items.explanation: When the audio is cut or edited, use [sound cut] on a separate line or on the same line, wherever the sound cut was done.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: [sound cut]

items.stem: A speaker uses a language other than English. How is it marked?
options: [foreign language] or a named language such as [French language], if it can be identified
items.explanation: If a foreign language or word is spoken, mark it as [foreign language] or [French language], [German language] and so on if it can be identified.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: foreign language

items.stem: A speaker says 'carpe diem' and 'alea jacta est'. How are these written?
options: Researched and written out properly, not tagged as foreign language
items.explanation: Authors, titles, personalities and common sense things are an exception to the foreign-language rule and must always be researched: carpe diem, Jacques Chirac, Frederic Chopin, alea jacta est.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Sound events: research authors, titles and expressions

items.stem: Which of these may never be bolded in a GoTranscript transcript?
options: Ordinary words, proper nouns and the first word of a paragraph
Speaker labels and marks with time-stamps
items.explanation: Everything with a time-stamp should be bolded, and nothing else besides the speaker labels and marks with time-stamps should be bolded.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: what must and must not be bolded

items.stem: How are numbers written in a GoTranscript transcript?
options: Single-digit numbers are spelled out, all other numbers use numerals
Single-digit numbers use numerals, all other numbers are spelled out
items.explanation: Spell out single-digit numbers and use numerals for all other numbers: zero, nine, 10, and so on.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: spell out single-digit numbers

items.stem: A sentence mixes a small number and a large number: 'I have nine apples and 10 pears.' How is it written?
options: All numbers in numerals: 'I have 9 apples and 10 pears'
All numbers spelled out: 'I have nine apples and ten pears'
Small numbers spelled out, large numbers in numerals
It depends on how the speaker said them
items.explanation: If a sentence combines small [0-9] and large numbers [10 and up], transcribe all numbers in numerals.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: combination of small and large numbers

items.stem: Which set of money amounts is written exactly as the guidelines require?
items.explanation: Money is an exception to the number rule and is written with numerals and the currency symbol: $1, $1.5 million, $1,000.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, money

items.stem: How are the slang amounts '1 grand', '5 bucks' and '8 quid' written?
items.explanation: The guidelines give these money conversions: 1 grand is 1,000, 5 bucks is $5, and 8 quid is £8.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, money (1 grand, 5 bucks, 8 quid)

items.stem: A speaker says 'half a million dollars'. How is it written?
items.explanation: The guidelines list half a million dollars as $500,000 among the money exceptions.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, money (half a million dollars is $500,000)

items.stem: How are years and eras written?
items.explanation: Years and eras are an exception to the number rule and are written as numerals: '90s, 1990s.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, years and eras

items.stem: How is an age such as 'in her seventies' written?
items.explanation: Age is an exception to the number rule: 70s, 30s.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, age

items.stem: How are percentages written?
items.explanation: Percentages are an exception to the number rule and use the percent sign: 0.2%, 100%.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, percentages

items.stem: Which set of measurements follows the guidelines?
options: 3 degrees, 12 feet, 8 centimeters, 7 pounds, 1.5 kilos, 28 square meters
Three degrees, twelve feet, eight centimeters, seven pounds
3 degrees, 12 feet, 8 centimeters, 7 pounds, 1.5 kilos, 28 square metres
3 degree, 12 foot, 8 centimeter, 7 pound, 1.5 kilo, 28 square meter
items.explanation: Measurements are an exception to the number rule and keep numerals: 3 degrees, 12 feet, 8 centimeters, 7 pounds, 1.5 kilos, 28 square meters.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, measurements

items.stem: How is a mathematical formula written?
options: x equals x plus 2, x cubed equals 8
items.explanation: Mathematical equations and formulas are an exception to the number rule: x = x + 2 or x ^ 3 = 8.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, mathematical equations and formulas

items.stem: How is the fraction 'one third' written?
items.explanation: Fractions are an exception to the number rule and are written as 1/3.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, fractions

items.stem: Which pair of contact details is written exactly as the guidelines require?
options: nine one two one zero and one two three four five six seven eight nine
items.explanation: Postal code is 91210 and phone number is 123-456-789, both listed as exceptions to the number rule.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, postal code and phone number

items.stem: How are Bible citations written?
options: John one, verses two to three
items.explanation: Bible citations keep numerals and use a colon: John 1:2-3, and for multiple citations John 1:3; 3:16; 6:14, 44.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions, Bible citation

items.stem: How are times of day written?
options: Half past two in the afternoon
items.explanation: Times of day and dates always capitalize AM and PM: 2:45 PM, 5:00 AM.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Times of the day and dates: always capitalize AM and PM

items.stem: How is a time said with o'clock written?
items.explanation: When using o'clock, spell out the numbers: eleven o'clock.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Times of the day: when using o'clock, spell out the numbers

items.stem: Which title is capitalized correctly?
options: Grade 8, Section B, Chapter 1, Article VI
grade 8, section b, chapter 1, article vi
Grade Eight, Section B, Chapter One, Article VI
Grade 8, section B, chapter 1, Article VI
items.explanation: Capitalize nouns followed by numbers or letters that are part of a series: Grade 8, Section B, Chapter 1, Article VI.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: capitalising nouns that are part of a series

items.stem: Which reference is written correctly?
items.explanation: Smaller divisions are not capitalized: page 1, paragraph 7.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: do not capitalize smaller divisions

items.stem: Which sentence follows the number rules exactly?
options: I had nine tickets and 12 seats.
I had nine tickets and twelve seats.
I had 9 tickets and twelve seats.
items.explanation: The sentence combines a small number and a large number, so all numbers are written in numerals: 9 tickets and 12 seats.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: single-digit numbers and the combination rule

items.stem: Which list uses the number exceptions correctly?
options: nineties, seventies, 12 foot, 0.2 percent, one third
items.explanation: Years, age, measurements, percentages and fractions are all exceptions to the number rule and keep numerals.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Numbers: exceptions for readability

items.stem: When does the guidelines say to use a double dash (--)?
options: For a change of thought (a false start), a speech error, or an incomplete sentence
Only for a change of thought
items.explanation: Use double dashes when there is a change of thought (false start) or a speech error, or to mark an incomplete sentence.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Double dashes or a single dash

items.stem: In full verbatim, a speaker says 'I went to the bank on Thursday-- no, Friday.' How is the speech error written?
options: I went to the bank on Thursday - no, Friday.
I went to the bank on Thursday-- no, Friday.
I went to the bank on Thursday... no, Friday.
I went to the bank on Thursday, no, Friday.
items.explanation: A speech error is written with double dashes, exactly as in the guidelines' example: 'I went to the bank on Tu-Thursday-- no, Friday.'
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Double dashes: FV speech error

items.stem: A speaker stops mid-sentence: 'I wanted to say something but--'. How is the incomplete sentence written?
options: I wanted to say something but-
I wanted to say something but...
I wanted to say something but--
I wanted to say something but
items.explanation: An incomplete sentence ends with a double dash, whatever the verbatim type. This is also why a sentence ending in a double dash needs no other punctuation mark.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Double dashes: incomplete sentence

items.stem: Speaker 1 is interrupted but carries on: 'I thought he was-' / 'Speaker 2: Yeah.' / 'Speaker 1: -gone.' Which mark is used?
options: A double dash at the end and at the start
An ellipsis at the end and at the start
A single dash at the end and at the start
No mark, because the sentence continues
items.explanation: Use a single dash when the speech is interrupted in a conversation but the speaker continues his thought.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Single dash: the speech is interrupted but the speaker continues

items.stem: In full verbatim, how are a stutter and a repetition marked?
options: With a single dash: 'Why is this m-m-moist?' and 'Why is this- why is this moist?'
With a double dash: 'Why is this m--m-moist?'
items.explanation: The guidelines' full verbatim examples use a single dash for stutters and repetitions: 'Why is this m-m-moist?' and 'Why is this- why is this moist?'
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Single dash: FV stutter and FV repetition

items.stem: Which punctuation introduces a direct quotation?
items.explanation: Double quotation marks are used whenever there is a direct quotation, and quotations are introduced by a comma, not a colon.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Quotation marks

items.stem: Where does a comma belong in relation to closing quotation marks?
items.explanation: Commas and periods always go inside the quotation marks.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Quotation marks: commas and periods go inside

items.stem: She asked, 'Can you help me?' Where does the question mark go?
items.explanation: The question mark is inside the quotation because the quotation itself is a question.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Quotation marks: the question mark goes inside

items.stem: The whole sentence is a question and it contains a quotation: 'Did she say "I am late"?' Where does the question mark go?
items.explanation: If the rest of the sentence is a question containing a quotation, then the question mark goes outside of the quotation marks.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Quotation marks: question mark outside when the sentence is the question

items.stem: How is a speaker's inner thought written? 'And then I thought to myself, "What if I can't make it?"'
options: Without quotation marks, because it is inner thought
As a direct quotation, because internal dialogues are seen as direct quotations as well
items.explanation: Internal dialogues are seen as direct quotations as well, and are introduced by a comma.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Quotation marks: internal dialogues are direct quotations

items.stem: How is this written: 'The man said that he was in a hurry.'
options: With quotation marks around 'he was in a hurry'
Without quotation marks, because it is an indirect quotation
With a single dash around the reported words
items.explanation: Do not use quotation marks in indirect quotations, where the speaker paraphrases what has been said.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Quotation marks: no quotation marks in indirect quotations

items.stem: When quoting a complete sentence, how is its first word written?
items.explanation: When quoting, the first word of a complete sentence should be capitalized.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Quotation marks: the first word of a quoted complete sentence

items.stem: Which group of titles must be italicized?
options: Film, book, magazine and song titles, artworks, plays, TV and radio programs, and foreign expressions
Company names and social media sites
The Bible and its books, and versions of it
items.explanation: Italicize film, book, magazine and song titles, as well as artworks, plays, TV and radio programs, and foreign expressions.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Italics: what to italicize

items.stem: Which group does NOT need italicizing?
options: Social media sites, company names, the Bible, books within it, and other sacred writings
items.explanation: There is no need to italicize social media sites, company names, the Bible, books within the Bible, versions of it or other sacred writings.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Italics: what not to italicize

items.stem: How is the abbreviation 'United States of America' written?
items.explanation: Abbreviations and acronyms should not contain dashes or periods: right is USA, PhD, wrong is U.S.A., Ph.D.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Abbreviations and acronyms

items.stem: How are the abbreviations 'Dr.' and 'Mrs.' written?
options: Dr., Mrs. in American English; Dr, Mrs without the period in British English
They are always written in full
items.explanation: Right American English: Dr., Mrs. Right British English: Dr, Mrs without the period. The guidelines also ask for US (American) spelling unless the client asks otherwise.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Abbreviations: American and British English

items.stem: How should a brand or organisation name that has a well-known capitalisation be written?
items.explanation: Always research the proper capitalisation, for example iPhone, UCLA and SaaS.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Always research the proper capitalization

items.stem: How is a spoken web address written?
options: w w w dot facebook dot com slash groups slash gotranscript
items.explanation: Always write links like this: www.facebook.com/groups/gotranscript. Never write it like this: w w w dot facebook dot com slash groups slash gotranscript.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Always write links like this

items.stem: Which passage follows the quoting and italics rules?
options: She said, "I watched an episode of Friends the other day," and smiled.
She said: "I watched an episode of Friends the other day" and smiled.
She said, "I watched an episode of friends the other day" and smiled.
She said: 'I watched an episode of Friends the other day,' and smiled.
items.explanation: A direct quotation is introduced by a comma rather than a colon, and the title of the TV program is italicized.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Quotation marks and italics

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: What must an applicant do to pass the first part of the GoTranscript transcription test?
options: Score at least 80% on the guidelines quiz
Complete the guidelines quiz with 100% correct answers; each question can have one or more correct answers
Complete the guidelines quiz and then a written essay
items.explanation: To apply for a transcriber position you must complete the quiz with 100% correct using the guidelines, and each question can have one or more correct answers.
items.reference: GoTranscript step-by-step guide to taking the GoTranscript transcription test - the quiz

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: How must the second part of the GoTranscript test, the test job, be transcribed?
options: Full verbatim with a timestamp every 2 minutes
Clean verbatim with a timestamp every time the speaker changes
items.explanation: The test job needs to be done in clean verbatim without timestamping. You type everything you hear, using the transcription rules.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - finish our test job (clean verbatim; no timestamping needed)

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: Before submitting the test job, what does the guidelines ask an applicant to do?
items.explanation: If you are interested in working with us, you need to read the provided instructions again and then finish the test job.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Interested? read the provided instructions again

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: How long can the review of a submitted test job take?
items.explanation: Once you send the completed test, the reviewing process can take up to 60 days, after which you get an email saying whether you passed.
items.reference: GoTranscript step-by-step guide to taking the GoTranscript transcription test - the reviewing process

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: Which accuracy band does a rating of 4 cover?
items.explanation: The rating scale is 5 from 96% to 100% accuracy, 4 from 92% to 95%, 3 from 88% to 91%, 2 from 83% to 87% and 1 from 0% to 82%.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Ratings which are given by editors

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: When is a new transcriber removed from the team?
options: After three transcriptions with an average rating of 3.6 or lower
After five transcriptions with an average rating of 4 or lower
items.explanation: If a new transcriber finishes 3 transcriptions and has a 3.6 or lower average rating, he or she will be removed from the team.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - new transcriber removal rule

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: Besides accuracy, what do editors rate a transcription on?
options: Grammar mistakes and lack of research
items.explanation: Along with accuracy, editors rate files based on grammar mistakes and lack of research, and mistakes of that kind are harshly penalised.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - editors rate accuracy, grammar and research

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: What happens if a transcriber does not prepare transcriptions according to the guidelines?
options: The file is returned for rework
The rate for the file is reduced
Nothing, as long as the transcript is readable
The transcriber might be removed from the team of transcribers
items.explanation: If you do not prepare the transcriptions according to these requirements, you might be removed from the team of transcribers.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - consequence of not following the requirements

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: What can a transcriber do if their average rating is better than 4.5?
options: Move to a higher paying client
items.explanation: If your average rating is better than 4.5, you can try to become an editor.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - becoming an editor

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: What happens first when a client uploads a file?
options: The transcriber is paid for the file
The client requests a specific format from the transcriber
The file appears in the transcriber's queue with no notification
The transcriber receives an e-mail, then chooses the files on the transcription jobs page
items.explanation: Every time a client uploads a file you receive an e-mail, then you go to the transcription jobs page and choose the files you want to transcribe. There you also see the turnaround time, the text format (clean or full verbatim) and the timestamping type if one is required.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - how transcription jobs reach the transcriber

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: How are transcribers paid for their work?
options: Payments are made every weekend, on Friday, and the stats page shows earnings per file
Per approved word, paid on the 15th
Only when the client pays GoTranscript
items.explanation: After your transcription is uploaded you see your current earnings on the stats page; payments are made every weekend, on Friday, and the statistics page shows what you earned for each file.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - earnings, statistics page and payments

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: The audio quality of a job is terrible. What should the transcriber do?
options: Transcribe it as best they can without comment
Report it, and GoTranscript contacts the client and provides a refund for that file
Cancel the job and wait for a replacement
Ask the client to re-upload the file
items.explanation: Sometimes the quality of audio or video files is horrible, so let us know about that; GoTranscript will contact the client and provide a refund for that file.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - reporting bad audio quality

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: Which spelling rule applies to GoTranscript work?
options: British spelling, because the editors are based in the UK
US (American) spelling; other spelling only if the client asks in the comments, and use Grammarly
Any spelling, as long as it is consistent
The spelling used by the audio speaker
items.explanation: Use US (American) spelling. Only use a different spelling if a client asks for it in the comments, and use Grammarly to check the result.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Use US (American) spelling (use Grammarly)

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: A speaker says 'and so on and so forth'. When may the transcriber drop 'et cetera'?
options: Never, unless the client asks otherwise in the comment section
Whenever the transcript would be too long
items.explanation: Do not remove the word et cetera unless the client asks otherwise in the comment section.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Do not remove the word et cetera

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: The audio contains a curse word. How is it transcribed?
options: Word for word, exactly as spoken
items.explanation: If there are curse words in the audio, transcribe them word for word.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - curse words

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: A client dictates formatting instructions while speaking: 'make a new paragraph there' and 'make that a bullet point'. What should the transcriber do?
options: Transcribe the instructions and then apply them
Follow them where possible but never transcribe them; a bullet point is written as a dash
Ask the client to put the instructions in the comment field
items.explanation: Customer dictation of formatting instructions should be followed when possible, but never transcribed. Do not type out the instruction, and use a dash for a bullet point.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - customers dictating formatting instructions

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: A speaker spells a name aloud: 'My name is Anna. A-N-N-A.' How is it written in an interview transcript?
options: Always omitted, because it is redundant
Included, except in dictation type transcripts
Written in brackets in every transcript type
Included only in full verbatim files
items.explanation: Do not put the spelled-out letters in if it is a dictation type transcript, but do put them in for all other types of transcripts.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - speakers spelling a word or a name

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: A speaker makes a grammatical error. What must the transcriber do?
options: Leave the error uncorrected, never paraphrase, and never add a [sic] tag
Paraphrase the sentence so it reads better
items.explanation: Never paraphrase or reconstruct the speech. Do not correct grammatical errors made by the speakers, and do not use the [sic] tag.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: never paraphrase, no [sic] tag

items.domain: The Test Job, Ratings and House Style
items.stem: A speaker pronounces 'niche' as 'nitche'. How should the transcriber write it?
items.explanation: Always use the correct spelling for misspoken words. The guidelines' example turns 'nitche' into 'niche'.
items.reference: GoTranscript transcriber guidelines - Major rules: correct spelling for misspoken words
